claims.text: Integrating ab initio phonon-scattering descriptors into a machine-learning framework will improve prediction accuracy for low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys relative to mean-field or effective-medium models.
The relevant HEAs exhibit complex, disordered multicomponent compositions.
The relevant HEAs exhibit local lattice distortions.
The relevant HEAs exhibit anharmonic vibrational modes.
The proposed model will incorporate ab initio descriptors including local vibrational-mode distributions and anharmonicity metrics.
The model will be calibrated using targeted experimental thermal-conductivity measurements.
The approach is applicable to HEAs containing at least five elements, with each element present at approximately 5–35 at.%.
The approach is applicable between approximately 300 K and 800 K.
Phonon scattering dominates thermal transport in the stated HEAs between approximately 300 K and 800 K.
Local vibrational characteristics and anharmonicity mediate phonon scattering in a disordered HEA lattice.
Ab initio descriptors allow the machine-learning model to learn nonlinear relationships between local lattice disorder and phonon-scattering efficiency.
Learning these nonlinear relationships will reduce phonon-thermal-conductivity prediction error relative to traditional models.
The proposed model will predict phonon thermal conductivity with less than 10% discrepancy from experiment.
The proposed model will reduce prediction error by more than 50% relative to conventional approaches.
Conventional mean-field or effective-medium approaches generally have prediction errors exceeding 20% for disordered HEAs.
Improved accuracy is expected only within the stated 300–800 K temperature and compositional regimes.
Predictions may deviate substantially under cryogenic conditions or for alloys with extreme defect concentrations.
The magnitude of improvement may vary among alloy systems and synthesis conditions.
The benchmark will compare model predictions with measurements at multiple temperatures, including 300 K, 500 K, and 800 K.
The approach is falsified if more than 50% of tested alloys deviate from predictions by over 10%, or if overall average error exceeds 20%.
